Background and context to
AUSTRAC claim

November 2019

A. Our role in relation to financial crime

* Asa major bank, our role is to help AUSTRAC and the Government to fight financial and
other serious crime.

+ We need to have systems and controls in place to prevent our services being exploited
for financial crime and other serious crime.

* These processes include:
o Assessing and mitigating money laundering and terrorism financing risks we face
o Monitoring transactions and conducting customer due diligence
» Providing AUSTRAC with information about financial transactions
o Telling AUSTRAC about any suspicious customers or activity

* Financial crime is a serious threat to our society. Our role in supporting AUSTRAC and
law enforcement to fight serious crime is critical.

B. AUSTRAC’s allegations

+ AUSTRAC is a financial intelligence agency and a regulator. It has been investigating
aspects of Westpac’s AML/CTF policies, procedures and oversight.

* On Wednesday 20 November, AUSTRAC commenced civil proceedings against
Westpac, alleging contraventions of its obligations under the Anti-Money Laundering and
Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth).

+ AUSTRAC's allegations fall into six main categories:
o IFTI reporting failures
oc Associated tracing information failures
o Record keeping failures
o Correspondent banking due diligence failures
o AML/CTF program failures

o Ongoing customer due diligence failures (regarding identifying, mitigating and
managing child exploitation risks)

i A ro —— a ———
We explain some of AUSTRAC's allegations below including parts of AUSTRAC’s claims in
relation to IFTI reporting, correspondent banking, and ongoing customer due diligence
(regarding identifying, mitigating and managing child exploitation risks).

IFTIs

AUSTRAC.
alleges that
Westpac failed
to report over
19.5 million
IFTIs.

Westpac is required to report to AUSTRAC all
international funds transfer instructions (or IFTIs) that it
receives or sends.

When senior management became aware of the failure
to report a large number of IFTIs over a long period of
time, Westpac promptly self-reported this to AUSTRAC
in August 2018 and began to remediate on an urgent
basis.

Since that time, we have worked with AUSTRAC to
report the missing IFTIs. 99.99% of these IFTIs have
now been reported with a small number of remaining
IFTIs to be reported by the end of November. The
majority of non-reported IFTIs in the claim concern
batch instructions received by Westpac through one
WIB product (called the Australasian Cash
Management product).

The majority of IFTIs were from two global
correspondent banks, making payments to Australian
beneficiaries on behalf of clients of the correspondent
banks. The majority of the payments were low value
recurring payments made by foreign government
pension funds and corporates, which had a low risk
profile.

We have closed the relevant ACM product.

We have addressed the technical root causes of the
non-reporting and uplifted our governance and
processes in relation to IFTI reporting.

Correspondent
banking due
diligence

AUSTRAC.
alleges that
Westpac failed
to adequately
assess the risk
of, and conduct
due diligence
into, 16 of its
correspondent
banking
relationships

We are reviewing the allegations in relation to Westpac’s
correspondent banking due diligence. We have been
working constructively with AUSTRAC for a number of
years in relation to our correspondent banking
arrangements. This has included making changes to our
correspondent banking program to address
recommendations made by AUSTRAC in its 2016
Compliance Assessment Report into Westpac's
correspondent banking controls. We have been and
continue to enhance our Correspondent Banking Standard
and practices as part of a program of work established to
review and uplift our AML/CTF Program.

Ongoing
customer due
diligence in
relation to
financial
indicators of
potential child
exploitation risk
in relation to
payments to the
Philippines and
South East Asia

AUSTRAC
alleges that
Westpac failed to
carry out
appropriate due
diligence on 12
customers, with a
view to identifying,
mitigating and
managing the
known risks of
child exploitation.

For a number of years, Westpac has worked closely with
AUSTRAC in addressing the risks of child exploitation and
other serious crime.

The LitePay product was launched in 2016. LitePay is a low
value payments channel (for payments up to $3000) which
was designed to provide customers with a low-cost solution
for transferring money to a range of countries with a fixed fee
of $5 per transfer. The product was introduced for a range of
reasons including to enable customers to send money to
family members living outside Australia.

The LitePay product was launched with detection monitoring
scenarios in August 2016 prepared with regard to industry
guidance issued by AUSTRAC at the time.

In December 2016, AUSTRAC issued Westpac’s financial
crime team with industry guidance regarding key indicators
for the purchase of child exploitation material involving
international funds transfers to the Philippines and South
East Asia.

Westpac continued with its existing detection monitoring
standards. Westpac failed to update its detection monitoring
scenarios to reflect this revised guidance until June 2018,
when it introduced the revised transaction monitoring
scenario across LitePay payments to the Philippines.

In October 2019, Westpac extended the revised transaction
scenario to SWIFT channel payments to the Philippines.

While Westpac had monitoring processes over the 12
customers prior to the receipt of AUSTRAC'’s claim, and had
filed suspicious matter reports for each of the 12 customers
(either in response to alerts from the detection scenarios in
place at the time or from other processes and reviews),
Westpac acknowledges it should have implemented more
robust transaction monitoring earlier than it did. This would
have generated more suspicious matter reports to
AUSTRAC.

AUSTRAC's Statement of Claim states that the detection
scenarios we now have in place for LitePay are appropriate
to detect known child exploitation risks involving the
Philippines.

During the course of its investigation, AUSTRAC has
requested information and documents in relation to a number
of customers. Westpac first learnt AUSTRAC had specific
concerns in relation to the 12 customers on 15 November
2019 and was not provided with any specific allegations until
it received AUSTRAC’s Statement of Claim.

Westpac accepts responsibility for the issues that have occurred. Westpac has identified the
need to improve financial crime management, based on issues identified by its business,
financial crime and internal audit teams over a number of years. In response, Westpac has
taken many actions to improve its financial crime management, including:
* dealing with and fixing individual issues, including the IFT non-reporting issues;
* making a significant investment to consolidate different financial crime systems into a
single, Group-wide technology system;
* more than doubling its internal resourcing dedicated to financial crime to 750 people.
Over the next 12 months we expect to add a further 200 people to this area;
* making changes to the management of its financial crime team and establishing a
Board Risk & Compliance Committee approved Financial Crime Strategic Plan in
2019, which has been shared with AUSTRAC;
* establishing a stand-alone executive level Financial Crime Committee, to oversee the
Group's Financial Crime governance;
* conducting Financial Crime workshops with the Board Risk & Compliance
Committee; and
* engaging various external consultants and advisors to perform assurance reviews
over aspects of the Group's financial crime processes and to advise on changes to
its program and approach.

The Board, CEO and management team are fully committed to taking all steps necessary to
urgently close any remaining gaps, and to accelerate the completion of the Financial Crime
Strategic Plan. Based on its current understanding, the Board does not believe that there has
been any indifference by any member of the Executive Team, including the CEO, but accepts
that Westpac has fallen short of its own and regulatory expectations and that a detailed review
is required to investigate the facts alleged by AUSTRAC.

The Westpac Board understands the gravity of the issues presented by AUSTRAC and
reiterates its deep sorrow for failings by Westpac.

The Federal Court of Australia has today ordered
Westpac to pay a $1.3 billion penalty for its breaches of
the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism
Financing Act 2006 (AML/CTF Act).

The penalty imposed is the highest civil penalty in
Australian history, reflecting the seriousness of
compliance failings by Westpac.

AUSTRAC CEO Nicole Rose PSM said the outcome
today sends a strong statement to Westpac and the
financial sectors we regulate that they are obliged by
law to take their obligations seriously or significant
penalties will be applied.

“Financial institutions must ensure they have strong
compliance systems, processes and resources in place
to protect the Australian community and their
businesses from criminals and criminal threats.”

“To maintain public confidence in Australia's financial
system and prevent future non-compliance, AUSTRAC
will not hesitate to take action when these obligations
are not met. This is aligned with AUSTRAC’s role and
community expectations.”
Ms Rose said it is critical industry recognise they are
first line of defence against criminals, and failing to meet
their AML/CTF obligations puts the safety of our
community at risk.

“AUSTRAC is committed to working collaboratively with
Westpac and all regulated businesses to support them
to understand and meet their obligations to protect
Australia’s financial system from criminal threats.”

Westpac continues to partner with AUSTRAC to assist
AUSTRAC and law enforcement agencies to stop
financial crime, including as a member of AUSTRAC’s
private-public partnership the Fintel Alliance.

About AUSTRAC

AUSTRAC (the Australian Transaction Reports and
Analysis Centre) is the Australian Government agency
responsible for detecting, deterring and disrupting
criminal abuse of the financial system to protect the
community from serious and organised crime.

Through strong regulation, and enhanced intelligence
capabilities, AUSTRAC collects and analyses financial
reports and information to generate financial
intelligence.

caption:
No wonder so many women feel caught between who they are and who they think they need to be.

>> Speak up and you’re “too much.”

>> Stay quiet and you’re a people pleaser.

Strong OR soft.

Ambitious OR nurturing.

Career OR family.

As if we must constantly choose one side or the other. No wonder there is a huge spike in symptoms like attention disorders. Our attention is constantly being split, yet we just write it off as “mum life”

One of the concepts we use in leadership is understanding healthy tension.

The ability to hold two opposing truths at the same time.

To be kind and direct.

To have boundaries and compassion.

To be ambitious and deeply present.

To care about performance and wellbeing.

And if my leaders at reading this, I mentally laugh and also apologise for thinking that when I became a leader I now “knew” — but the learning never stops.

That’s one of the main differences between leadership and management. 

What if leadership isn’t about choosing?
What if it’s about integration?

I’ve spent over a decade working across banking, learning, leadership development and executive coaching.

One thing I’ve noticed is that many women think there’s something wrong with them because leadership feels uncomfortable. But when you zoom out, the discomfort makes sense.

The first female branch manager at the bank I worked for was appointed in 1974.

The bank opened its door in the 1850s.

Think about that.

For more than a century, leadership was largely modelled by men because they were the ones allowed to occupy those positions. 

Before this, women were only allowed to type or answer phones. During this time, there were also guns in the bottom drawers.

Times change.
Humans evolve. 

And this era is asking us to lean into what leadership looks like when success includes wellbeing.

When authority includes humanity.

When ambition is no longer disconnected from values.

1+3 =4 but so does 2+2 

Just because it looks and feels different, doesn’t mean it’s wrong. 

✨

#femalefounded
#womeninleadership
#senseofher
#senseofself
#selfleadership

caption:
Day 318

Recently a police investigator asked me:

“Why is it so hard to get information from the bank? I thought we were on the same team.”

And I had to tell him, that’s the problem. People assume everyone is working towards the same objective.

They’re not.

Customers want their money protected.
Police want crime investigated.
Banks are incentivised to protect the bank.

The system isn’t broken. It’s producing exactly what it was designed to produce.

The question isn’t whether banks care.

The question is:
Why is it legal for banks to protect their own money with more security measures than customer money? 

If banks are more resourced, have the tech to protect themselves, why not everyone else too?

caption:
When I led teams in a bank contact centre, if a customer hung up and you needed time to document the interaction, investigate something further or update notes, you pressed a button called call work.

The longer you spent there, the more visible it became to leaders.

At one point, if you were in call work for too long, your name would start flashing on a manager’s screen.

Nobody ever said -
“Don’t spend time understanding the customer.”

But humans learn quickly what matters. 
20 seconds of call work. 

So when the human has a choice to prioritise investigating customer accounts or getting the customer off the phone, what do you think they choose?

If you’re measured on speed, you’ll optimise for speed.
If you’re measured on curiosity, you’ll optimise for curiosity.
If you’re measured on customer outcomes, you’ll optimise for outcomes.

So, what if culture isn’t created by values, like we’ve been led to believe?

What if culture is simply the behaviour a system rewards repeatedly?

It makes sense as to why the financial system is in crisis at the moment.

caption:
Happy birthday and tanti auguri 🎈

To our Nonno, Antonio LoCastro 🇮🇹

Today, he would have turned 103 and although he may no longer be physically with us, I carry him with me every day as we navigate the unknown.

At just 19 years old, he was called to serve in the war. When I think about that now, I can’t even begin to imagine what he experienced.

What I do know is that he was a grafter, and during the war that was a vital skill for survival. It always came so naturally to him that he never really considered it a skill, rather something that he was good at. He became known for his craftsmanship and his ability to graft plants together to create new varieties of fruit — like what we now know as a nashi pear 🍐 

After the war, with little opportunity left in his village, he made the courageous decision to leave everything he knew. At 46 years old, without speaking a word of English, he packed his bags with my Nonna, my dad and my uncle, boarded a boat, for 28 days, and came to Australia with the promise of something better.

To create a better future.

He sacrificed his present for ours.

My dad carried that legacy forward.

My Nonno rarely spoke about the war. But as I got older, I began translating his documents and learning more about the life he lived before Australia. The more I learn, the more I understand where my determination comes from. He survived extraordinary hardship so that future generations could have security and opportunity.

He was such a fighter, and survived some extreme conditions to get us to where we are today, which is why I now take on that leadership to continue to demand symmetry for a system that is out of date, and if they same security applied between bank and consumer, we wouldn’t even need to have his conversation.

caption:
Imagine seeing someone drown in the ocean and decide to judge and gossip about the way they asked for help or how they survived. 

Yet, this is what happens. 

When life throws you challenges to move through, the people around you will react because of the change of dynamic in relationship. 

That change being you needing to turn your energy inward, and those around you experience the reaction of that. Like; being around less, not because of a lack of love, but because the allocation of resources some periods of life require. 

It’s in this moment that you will face the uncomfortable truth of who was there for you, as a whole, and who was there for you, for what you provided for them. 

It sucks.

But, it’s human behaviour. 

The good news is that two things can be true. 

The space of who you thought would be there can be uncomfortable, but at the same time, it shows you what matters most. 

Lastly, unless you have walked the walk. The thoughts we have are just perceptions rather than reality. So we really need to be careful with “I would have done x if I were her” 

If we want to create a future where our kids feel like they belong, it starts with us role modelling that with our peers. 

Less judgement (emotional junkfood)
More empathy (emotional nutrition)

I really just wanted to make a complaint to dispute the unauthorised
transactions on our families account.

But here we are.
This is what happens in banking when there is no process.

Some of you may be thinking ‘why is there no process to get money
back for scams and only for fraud?’

Because banks have performance and reward metrics around their
money first, which is anything recorded as a financial gain or loss
takes priority. The way each layer of the organisation behaves is

based on their scorecard. All bank scorecards, as you would imagine,
prioritise financial gain or loss behaviour.

The issue impacting over 600,000 Australians right now is that
scams are recorded as a non-financial loss,
but fraud is recorded as a financial loss.

The banks mentality is that scams are entirely the customers fault,
yet with fraud it's the banks liability.

Why are they recorded differently?

Who presses the button in internet banking.
Fraud = hacked
Scam = customer pressed the button

The issue is, we are now in the Al era, and we are also dealing with
scammers who socially engineer whole ecosystems. To have this risk
100% on the customer is completely unethical and irresponsible.

Scams will ALWAYS be de-prioritised until there is pressure on the
banks to treat bank and customer money with the same levels of
security and protection.

Sign our petition to protect your parents, secure yours and your
families future. Our systems are not designed the way you imagine.
In theory yes, but in reality, humans are in the roles of the systems
which creates all different dynamics that can alter the intention of

the system we all know and rely on.

A friendly reminder to anyone in leadership. Trust is a symptom of upholding public promises. 

Organisational dysfunction, which a lack of trust is the foundation of, occurs when internal performance metrics are different to public promises. 

For example;

Because the tone is set from the top and trickles down. If scams are a non-financial loss on the banks balance sheet and fraud is a financial loss, every layer of the organisation, when setting performance goals, will prioritise bank revenue or bank loss over customer. 

Why? 

Because banking is a business.

19 August 2026

National Press Club
Address

The promise of all Labor governments — to strengthen the
system, to leave it better than we found it and to safeguard
it for future generations of Australians.

With this role comes the responsibility of safeguarding
what superannuation means for millions of Australians: the
promise of a dignified and secure retirement and the task
of protecting it for future generations.
Persistence, advocacy and courage in speaking out have
helped shine a light on serious failures within our financial
system. Some of the most important economic decisions
we make are not about the next year, but the next
generation.

Superannuation is one of Australia’s great nation-building
achievements. Today, superannuation underpins the
retirement security of millions of Australians and stands as
the foundation of our retirement income system.

As our superannuation system matures and more people
approach retirement, as balances grow and products
become more sophisticated, it must continue to evolve
alongside the Australians that it serves.
Our super system is amongst the largest in the world, but
for many, advocacy remains a work in progress as life
expectancy rises and as health care and aged care
become more complex and costly.

It is a system that is already supporting millions in
retirement, but preservation is constantly under threat from
short-sighted policies. Our system continues to face
challenges. Access to financial advice has shrunk, and bad
actors have become more sophisticated, attracted by
Australia’s huge pool of retirement savings.
Australia’s superannuation system will be strengthened
through better consumer protection, increased stability and
improved access to financial advice. These reforms will
help protect the promise of a dignified and secure
retirement for generations to come.

The collapses of Shield and First Guardian affected almost
12,000 Australians who invested more than $1 billion of
their retirement savings into those schemes. For many
people, the losses they have incurred represent most, or
even all, of their retirement savings they spent decades
building. These events exposed vulnerabilities across
multiple parts of the financial ecosystem.
They involved sophisticated and often predatory
lead-generation practices, advice arrangements that may
have failed the best interest duty, and managed investment
schemes alleged to have involved mismanagement,
conflicted conduct and potentially fraud.

We will make the financial system safer by strengthening
protections across the superannuation advice and
investment ecosystem. We will improve access to safe,
secure financial advice and guidance so that Australians
can navigate an increasingly complex retirement system
with greater confidence and provide meaningful protection
when all other measures have failed.
These reforms will help to build a financial system that is
safer, more resilient and more worthy of the trust that
Australians place in it.

What happens when the external auditor becomes part of the system its purpose is to audit?

That system no longer remains truely independent and puts the integrity of the financial system at risk 🚩

In May 2026, KPMG and Anthropic announced a global strategic partnership. KPMG is deploying Claude across its 276,000+ workforce, embedding Claude into its client-delivery technology, co-developing products with Anthropic, and becoming Anthropic’s preferred private-equity consultant.

Currently the government are currently reviewing the business structure of KPMG (as well as the other big 4) to assess if its still fit for purpose in the modern-digital era. 

Our journey over the last 425 days, shows how risks can be overlooked with the introduction of new technology 💸

The tool may be new to humans, but human behaviour has a pattern when new technology advances over time. Just like any other tech, growth purpose and strategy are absolutely essential, but so is sustainability, ethical responsibility, governance and leadership through a new environment. 

It’s negligent to put humans at risk of harm just for the sake of growth. We need to take the whole customer lifecycle into consideration when making decisions, particularly around the introduction of AI into financial services. 

300 Billion dollars customers have across the big 4 banks in deposit accounts, they watch your credit card like a hawk, they’ll call you as soon as you miss any lending payment, but because the law hasn’t been explicit until the enactment of the Scam Prevention Framework, the never watched your money for scams. 

This era is just as big as the introduction of internet banking and then mobile banking, we need to make sure we’re making decisions not just in the short term, but for the future of the industry.

The card surcharges dynamic between the RBA,
the ATO, the Treasurer and the Prime Minister explained.

Where are the bank leaders? 

The owners of the product and service.

Three weeks ago, the Reserve Bank of Australia announced changes to card surcharging.

Last week, the Australian Taxation Office announced plans to stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills.

Since then, the ATO has indicated that the change will be delayed until June 2027.

So, for now, credit card payments remain available.
But this raises some important questions

🔘 Does the ATO still incur processing fees when accepting credit card payments?

🔘 If customers are no longer charged a surcharge, who absorbs the cost?

🔘 Why do different rules apply between a government agency and a small business, such as your local coffee shop?

🔘And where are the banks, payment providers and product owners?

Removing a surcharge doesn’t necessarily remove the cost of processing a payment. 

It changes who pays that cost.

As Australia’s financial system continues to evolve, especially in the modern- digital era, transparency matters.

Consumers and businesses deserve to understand not just what is changing, but why, who benefits and who ultimately pays 💲

caption:
The psychology of visibility ✨

Looking through the lens of human behaviour, it is against our biology to be seen, to be visible. 

Humans are pack animals. Our survival instinct tells us to fit in or we’ll be kicked out of the tribe.

But sometimes, certain things or periods in life require us to become more visible. To get to where we need to go. 

For most of my career, I spoke publicly. 

PS; I was not a public speaker before that. I was the type person who’d face would go as red as a tomato 🍅 

I did it because I had a passion for learning and helping people, the role just so happened to be at the front of the room. 

“If this is what I need to do to get to where in need to go, then I guess we’re doing it” — I used to tell myself to psych myself up some days. 

Something I learnt as I grew in my role was that visibility can bring up the all kinds of thoughts and fears that encourage us to stay small. 

Fear of judgement.
Fear of failure.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of being misunderstood.

So we adapt.

We manage perceptions.
We seek approval.
We edit our expression.
We become who we think we need to be to belong.

And sometimes, without realising it, we begin confusing acceptance with authenticity.

This is where self-leadership becomes important.

Because the goal isn’t to become someone who no longer experiences fear, anxiety or self-doubt.

It’s to develop the capacity to experience those emotions without allowing them to determine who we are or how we show up.

Happy Sunday 🫶🏼

Let’s see what this week brings 🙃

AFCA takes on the new jurisdiction with
complaint volumes already at record levels.
AFCA’s 2025-26 Annual Review on rising
complaints shows it received 119,949
complaints in 2025-26, the third straight
year above 100,000. Over the same period,
scam-related complaints rose 12% to 6,706.
What the Scams Prevention
Framework means for AFCA

The federal government introduced the
SPF to strengthen consumer protections
across several sectors. Banking,
telecommunications, and digital platforms
are the first in scope, and AFCA will hear
scam complaints relating to all three.
In June 2026, the Assistant Treasurer and
Minister for Financial Services authorised
AFCA to handle external disputes over
scam losses. AFCA has since concluded its
consultation on the Scams Prevention
Framework rules that will govern those
cases.
The SPF builds on powers AFCA already
holds. Since 12 March 2026, ASIC-
approved rule changes covering receiving
banks and mule accounts have allowed it to
examine the role of receiving banks and
mule accounts in scam complaints.
What changes in ASIC’s RG
267 guidance

ASIC’s oversight of AFCA rests on specific
provisions of the Corporations Act 2001.
The current RG 267 guidance on AFCA
oversight sets out AFCA’s legislative and
governance requirements alongside ASIC’s
own powers and functions. The proposed
changes, released on 27 October 2026,
reflect AFCA’s expanded remit under the
SPF.
“This is the first substantive update to RG
267 since AFCA was established in 2018,”
ASIC said in its announcement.

ASIC has trimmed the guide to avoid
duplicating AFCA’s own rulebook, saying it
wants to “simplify the guidance and ensure
that it remains clear and current”.
References it considers essential to AFCA’s
operation and legal obligations stay in.

At the same time, Australians are facing higher repayments, rising mortgage stress, job cuts, offshoring and increasingly complex scam and complaint systems.

Senior leaders from ANZ, Westpac, NAB and Commonwealth Bank are appearing before a parliamentary committee.

They are being questioned about —
✔️ interest rates and lending
✔️ mortgage stress
✔️ scams and fraud protection
✔️ complaints and customer remediation
✔️ artificial intelligence
✔️ job cuts and offshoring
✔️ access to banking services
✔️ conduct and governance

Bank leaders answer questions publicly.

The committee can examine their decisions, test their explanations and place their responses on the public record. This matters because complex systems often protect themselves through complexity.

Public hearings help translate those systems back into questions people can understand:

▪️Who made the decision?
▪️Who benefited?
▪️Who carried the risk?
▪️And who is accountable when the system fails?

WHAT’S NEXT?
The committee can then report on what it heard and recommend where greater accountability, regulation or reform may be needed.

But scrutiny is only the beginning.

The real test is whether public questioning leads to measurable change for customers, employees and communities.

I’ll keep following the thread and translating what happens at the top into what it means for everyday Australians.

Because Australians deserve to know the truth about the systems and leaders they place their trust, money and livelihood in.

volatile global environment and the rapid escalation of Al-

Published twice a year, the report describes what APRA is
seeing in the international and domestic environments,
highlighting shocks and vulnerabilities that could affect the
Australian financial system.
Key findings include:

e Global financial markets are under pressure. A sharp
repricing could raise funding costs and reduce
investment values in Australia;

e = Alis creating new risks within institutions,
accelerating cyber and operational threats that
could have broader effects across the economy and
financial system. Reliance on common service
providers is also creating channels for widespread
disruption; and

e Housing prices have declined and lending activity
has slowed, but household and bank resilience
remain strong overall. Higher living costs are putting
household budgets under pressure, but most
households have substantial equity and repayment
buffers. High household indebtedness remains a key
vulnerability that could amplify a more severe
downturn.
“Our financial system is well placed to withstand this
turbulent period. Financial buffers and robust operations
provide a strong foundation for system resilience. Recent
stress testing, including APRA’s first System Risk Stress

capacity to absorb significant market and liquidity stress.

“But institutions and regulators also need practical
capabilities to manage crises that combine financial and
operational pressures. In line with our most recent
Corporate Plan, APRA will remain focused on ensuring our
banks, insurers and superannuation trustees are well-
prepared for financial and operational shocks, including
complex crises where multiple pressures emerge
simultaneously,” Mr Lonsdale said.
“Australia’s financial system remains resilient, but the risk
environment is becoming less forgiving.

and vulnerabilities in financial markets and critical
infrastructure could amplify future shocks. Rapid advances
in Al are supporting economic activity but also accelerating
cyber and operational threats and increasing reliance ona

require banks, insurers and superannuation trustees to have
financial strength, operational readiness and crisis
preparedness.
The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority
(APRA) is the prudential regulator of the financial
services industry. It oversees banks, mutuals,
general insurance and reinsurance companies, life
insurance, private health insurers, friendly
societies, and most members of the

Women's formal leadership is newer than
we think.

1974.

The year NAB appointed its first female
branch manager.

That was only 52 years ago.

The female leadership path is still being built.
Before then, women in banking
were largely employed as:

Typists.
Clerks.
Administrative support.

Close to the decisions—
but rarely entrusted
to make them.
That means women’s formal leadership
in Australian banking
is only around 50 years old.

One working lifetime.

We are not continuing
a well-established tradition.

We are still creating one.
Women entered institutions
that had already decided
what leadership looked like.

Authority was masculine.
Emotion was weakness.
Power moved from the top down.

To progress, women often had to learn
how to survive that culture.
And so began the double bind:

Be warm—and risk being overlooked.
Be assertive—and be called difficult.

Speak softly—and disappear.
Speak clearly—and be told
you are too much.
| know that tension personally.

| love leading.

| love creating rooms

that expand what people believe
is possible for them.

But being at the front
also makes you visible.

And visibility invites judgment.
| have been called:

Too loud.

Too sensitive.

Too opinionated.
Attention-seeking.

For a long time,
| wondered whether wanting influence
meant there was something wrong with me.
But attention was never
the destination.

It was the doorway.
Because to lead a room,
move an idea

or challenge a system—

someone first has to notice you.
| don't want to stand at the front
because | believe | am
the most important person in the room.

| stand there because
| know how to open the room.

And help other people
take up more space inside it.
The next era of leadership
does not need women
performing the same old model.

It needs leaders who can hold:

Authority and humanity.
Ambition and accountability.
Technology and relationship.
Power and responsibility.
So | am no longer proving

that | am safe

by pretending | don't want power.
| do want influence.

Not power over people.

The power to create conditions
in which more people find theirs.
Women have only been formally leading
in this world for around 50 years.

The path still feels unpaved
because, in many ways, it is.

Maybe we are not struggling
to fit the existing model.

Maybe we are here
to create what comes next.
Women weren't lacking leadership. They were
denied authority.

NAB head of retail banking and social media fan Ana
Marinkovic. Picture: Jake Nowakowski
It’s been quite a year for NAB’ publicity
hungry retail bank boss, Ana Marinkovic.

It all started with a glowing profile in the
Australian Financial Review about how she
arrived in Australia aged 13 after fleeing
war-torn Serbia, learned English as her
fourth language and rose to an executive
position at the big-four bank.

Impressive, inspiring stuff.
The same newspaper later roughed her up
over a vapid, Kamala Harris-inspired
thought leadership post she’d shared on AI-
slop bin LinkedIn, which had that familiar
sulfurous tang of Al-produced copy. Talk
about building ’em up to knock ’em down!

Oh, well. All publicity is good publicity,
right?

The past week has really tested that maxim,
with a series of vicious anonymous posts
shared by an ex-NAB employee setting
Instagram — and Australia’s wider banking
community — aflame.
Many of the messages concern the alleged
culture at the Andrew Irvine-run bank.

Almost all of them are impossible to verify
or cannot be repeated for legal reasons.
People really can just say anything on the
internet.
But one particular allegation made by the
account about Marinkovic caught our eye:
that she allegedly had a picture of Vladimir
Putin on her phone case. Bonkers, surely.

But then the account posted a photo of a
woman who looks a lot like Marinkovic,
wearing a white jacket with a black fur
hood, taking a selfie in a mirror — with one
hand partially covering a picture of a man
on the back of her phone who looks a lot
like the Russian despot.

It’s understood the image is fake. Maybe it
was produced by Al, too.

NAB wouldn't comment about the photo.
Or any of the other posts for that matter.
We are told the account has triggered
permanent panic stations in NAB’s Bourke
Street HQ, and lawyers have been called in
as anxious executives await what might be
posted next. As we say, anyone can say
anything on the internet.
Which brings us back to Marinkovic.
Margin Call discovered her — now deleted —
Instagram account, which was no stranger
to saying things on the internet. A lot of the
utterances related to interior design or
tennis (her son is a prodigy).

Hey everyone, 

My name is Dani LoCastro.

I spent 14 years working @nab and was made redundant the 6 times during my career. Today, I’m a mum of two young children, one of who lives with a disability. I also help care for my parents. My parents have been involved in a large-scale multi-bank financial crime and I’ve been advocating for their retirement estate back for 475 days ‼️‼️

I’ve become a full-time customer advocate. 
I’ve spent countless hours tracing transactions, preparing evidence, writing submissions and challenging decisions when families are left to navigate complex financial systems on their own.

Legal teams have called so I’d like to be prepared to fight for all of us, and to keep doing the work that comes after it.

Donations will help cover the practical costs of this work: 
✔️ preparing evidence and submissions
✔️seeking professional advice where needed, 
✔️ and making time to follow matters through. 

I’ll share updates on what the funds support while protecting the privacy of the people involved.

If you’re able to contribute, thank you. 

If you can’t, no pressure at all. We’re in a cost of living crisis so I completely understand. Sharing this page helps too. 

I believe customers and families deserve to be heard, taken seriously and given a fair chance to challenge a system that is no longer meeting the needs of its leaders, colleagues and customers in the modern-digital era. 

Let’s all work together to create a better financial future, in whatever way possible for you.

This is such a unique situation and, honestly, it could be
harnessed as a motivator, a reset, a definition of what
leadership is actually supposed to look like.

Imagine if the response was something like:

“Team, there's been a lot of discussion lately around
situations people have experienced when interacting with
me. Some of those accounts are incredibly difficult to read,
particularly where the experience described is completely
counter to what | believe | stand for and what | am trying to
achieve here.
nab

Where my humanity has not shone through, I’m genuinely
sorry that this is how some people remember their
experience with me.

I'm not interested in shifting blame or spending more time
than necessary dwelling on the past. What | am interested in
is what this has made me reflect on, what | can learn from it,
and what | need to change. Those reflections have led me to
X, Y and Z.”

Am | stupid for thinking this doesn't actually need a crisis
meeting where everyone scrambles to discredit a platform
that has, ironically, been created from many of the same
foundations the organisation claims to value?

Remember “Own It”?

Or does that one only apply when you're not talking about
people at the top?
nab

For those who've been around long enough, “Speak Up” used
to be one of those phrases that was everywhere. It wasn't
just about encouraging people to speak up — it was
supposedly about creating the safety and support required
when people actually DID.

Speak Up Culture

So... why is an anonymous Google form so popular?

Why have 1,000 people felt compelled to use an anonymous
platform to share their experiences?

Maybe because people have tried internal channels.

Maybe because people don't trust what happens after they
do.

Maybe because when employees see outcomes that appear
to include complainants being managed out, protected
characteristics being disregarded, or people seemingly being
rewarded despite allegations about their behaviour, the
message becomes pretty fucking clear:

Speak up — but understand the consequences (your job,
dignity, control of your truth)

Heartbeat is meaningless if the environment underneath it
doesn’t support honest feedback.
nab

You'd be a fool to take pride in “results” if those results are
being generated in an environment where senior leaders
influence what people see, how feedback is interpreted, or
whether people feel safe enough to provide it honestly.

And even if only 10% of the claims being shared on this page
turned out to be true — despite the inevitable response that
it’s all lies, disgruntled bankers having their moment, or
people looking for attention — you STILL have a systemic
problem.

Because 10% is a fucking enormous problem when you're
talking about an organisation this size.

The answer shouldn't be to discredit the messenger.

It should be to understand why people feel more comfortable
telling thousands of strangers than telling their own
employer.

Hot take:

Would any of this be tolerated if it was a colleague treating a
customer in the same way?
nab

Now this could be controversial, so hold onto your golf
loafers sweetie

Why is our industry becoming so fucking bland?

Where is the creativity?

“Oh shit, PR crisis. Quick, grab the playbook from 1980.”
Why not:

“Wow. This could be bad. So let’s actually do something
different and prove we are the difference in banking.”

Bring in the people who know how to fix the problem.
Redesign the whistleblower process. Build something
genuinely independent. Do it in collaboration with the people
who actually use these systems.

And why couldn't that involve colleagues, former colleagues,
external experts — even people who have experienced the
system first-hand? pretty sure Dani’s proven through this
page she'd be more than equipped to land the outcome you
need or even consult for you (oh wait, sorry forgot all the
consultants were axed! We don't need them, silly me)

Imagine turning the 1,000 voices on this page into actual
feedback that informs the redesign.
nab

Imagine taking something that currently looks like a
reputational disaster and turning it into one of the biggest
cultural reset opportunities the organisation has had in
years.

And that’s just one idea.

Seriously — how many people being paid $200k+ are REALLY
unable to come up with something more creative than “deny,
discredit, contain’? Otherwise known as how to snort blow
on company time

Because the alternative is continuing to feed the exact cycle
you're trying to stop.

And eventually that doesn’t just damage the organisation's
reputation. It damages people's faith in the entire industry.

Customers already have pretty fucking low expectations of
banks.

Don't give them another reason to lose whatever trust they
have left.
nab

Not another crisis-management playbook.

Not another exercise in protecting reputations.

A real reset.

And maybe, for once, NAB could actually lead the pack rather
than follow the same tired corporate mould of tear-stained
ELT culture, defensive messaging and pretending everything
is fine.

Because there is an opportunity here.

Please don't fucking waste it.
nab

Of course there are.

But come on.

When hundreds — potentially thousands — of people are
independently describing similar experiences, at some point
you have to stop asking whether every individual story is
perfectly accurate and start asking why the SAME THEMES
keep appearing.

Are we seriously going to write all of that off as coincidence?

Or are we going to call everyone Al like the Putin case?
Someone forgot Facebook circa 2014 exists @)

As someone who still stupidly believes in the heart of this
organisation, | genuinely hope this becomes a cultural reset.

Not another PR exercise.
nab

Love your work Dani —Hey— curious, Has the FSU touched
this at all? They seem to be pretty quiet for people who
wanted media galore for anyone restructured......

Hopefully I’m wrong because after all, unions are meant to
advocate for worker rights (so we're effectively doing their
job for them right?) not pander to the golf loafers of the
world. ;P
nab

HR should exist to support the business's people — not
simply protect whoever has the biggest TEC package when a
conduct issue lands on the table.

At some point we need to stop managing the optics and
actually change the fucking behaviour.

Because it is pathetic that 1,000 people have apparently felt
the need to take their experiences onto the internet just to
feel heard, valued or seen.

Admit you've made mistakes.

Every person makes them. Every business makes them.

The measure of an organisation isn’t whether it has made
mistakes.

It's whether it is capable of acknowledging them and doing
something different afterwards.

Instead of repeatedly cutting loose the little guy while
protecting the people with the biggest titles, salaries and
networks, how about we start selecting and rewarding
people based on actual leadership, capability and behaviour?

Not shoe size.

Not wallet depth.

about financial crime, another issue worth exposing is
Australia's longstanding regulatory failure in relation to
money laundering.

Until July 2026, Australia was among a handful of countries,
including Haiti and Madagascar, that had failed to implement
key international anti-money laundering standards covering
professions such as real estate agents, lawyers, and
accountants.

attention is given to the distortionary effects of illicit capital
entering our property market.

economic incentives. Criminal networks seeking to
legitimise illicit wealth can outbid legitimate purchasers

issue across the financial services industry that warrants

experience has created an inherent tension between
commercial objectives and effective financial crime
prevention.

networks. Compromised identities can be exploited to

Al Overview

Sense of Her is a viral Instagram account () run by former National Australia Bank
(NAB) employee Dani (Daniela) LoCastro that has published unverified allegations
about workplace culture and senior leaders at NAB.

Key Details

Who runs it: Melbourne-based Dani LoCastro, a former NAB staffer who left
in May 2025 after roughly 14 to 15 years in banking and claims she was made
redundant multiple times.

What it posts: Since early November 2026, the account has shared anecdotal
claims and rumours alleging bullying, nepotism, unqualified hires, affairs, drug
or alcohol use, and leadership dysfunction across NAB.

NAB's response: CEO Andrew Irvine emailed staff in late November 2026
calling the claims “untrue, unverified and potentially harmful," noting the bank
has offered to meet with LoCastro and urged staff to use NAB's KPMG-run
whistleblower hotline.

Meta's stance: NAB asked Instagram owner Meta to remove the account, but
Meta declined, citing a balance between freedom of expression and protecting
users from bullying and harassment.

Broader context: The controversy coincided with NAB's planned 2,500-job
restructuring and an accidental premature sending of automated
redundancy/access emails to staff.

decision.
